slides.title: From Yom Kippur War to Lebanese Civil War
slides.cap: Historical overview: From Yom Kippur War to Lebanese Civil War
slides.body:
Regional conflict shifted toward Lebanon as the PLO established an armed state-within-a-state after expulsion from Jordan. Lebanon's fragile sectarian system, inequality, and competing foreign patrons made confrontation increasingly likely.

Lebanese factions fought over political power and survival. Israel sought to stop cross-border attacks, while Syria, the PLO, Iran, and later Hezbollah pursued competing regional goals.

This background is essential to understanding Lebanese Civil War: the conflict emerged from accumulated security failures, political choices, and unresolved disputes rather than from a single isolated incident. The recorded indicators, including 1975-1990 (key detail), help convey the episode's scale and the pressures facing decision-makers.

slides.title: Bus Massacre and Civil War
slides.cap: Historical overview: Bus Massacre and Civil War
slides.body:
A shooting and retaliatory attack on a bus carrying Palestinians helped ignite sustained fighting between Christian militias and a coalition of Palestinian and Lebanese leftist forces.

For Israel, Lebanon's collapse mattered because armed organizations used the vacuum to build bases, fire across the border, and pull outside powers into the conflict. Israeli policy was shaped by the need to protect the Galilee while avoiding a permanent slide into Lebanon's internal war.

slides.title: Syrian Intervention
slides.body:
Syria sent forces into Lebanon, initially restraining Palestinian-leftist gains while seeking lasting control over Lebanese politics.

slides.title: Operation Litani
slides.body:
After the Coastal Road massacre, Israel invaded southern Lebanon to push PLO forces away from its border. UNIFIL was created, but the security problem remained unresolved.

slides.title: 1982 Lebanon War
slides.body:
Israel invaded after repeated conflict with the PLO and drove its leadership from Beirut. The campaign weakened the PLO in Lebanon but expanded Israel's entanglement in the civil war.

slides.title: Beirut Barracks Bombings
slides.body:
Suicide bombers killed 241 US and 58 French service members serving in the multinational force. The attacks accelerated the Western withdrawal.

slides.title: Hezbollah Emerges
slides.body:
Backed by Iran, Hezbollah consolidated as a powerful Shiite militia committed to armed resistance against Israel and to an Islamist political project in Lebanon.

markers.label: Taif
markers.description: The political settlement ended much of the civil war but did not disarm Hezbollah.

markers.label: Southern Lebanon
markers.description: The unresolved armed presence in the south became the next phase of Israel's Lebanon challenge.

slides.title: Taif Settlement and War's End
slides.cap: Historical overview: Taif Settlement and War's End
slides.body:
The Taif Agreement ended the main phase of Lebanon's civil war by rebalancing state power and bringing most militias under formal disarmament. Its central security flaw was the exception that allowed Hezbollah to keep its weapons while Syrian influence remained entrenched.

For Israel, that meant the war's end did not restore a stable northern frontier. The PLO's old position in Lebanon had been weakened, but an Iranian-backed organization with a long-term military project was left armed, politically protected, and able to turn southern Lebanon into the next pressure point.

title: Conflict Summary: Lebanese Civil War
sub: Final summary of Lebanese Civil War

markers.label: Lebanon
markers.description: The civil war ended formally, but foreign influence and Hezbollah's retained weapons left the border conflict unresolved.

slides.title: Conflict Summary: Lebanese Civil War
slides.cap: Historical overview: Conflict Summary: Lebanese Civil War
slides.body:
The civil war devastated Lebanon and entrenched Syrian and Iranian influence. Israeli operations disrupted PLO attacks but did not create a durable political settlement, while Hezbollah emerged as a stronger long-term threat. Taif ended general warfare without fully restoring state control over armed force.

Taken as a whole, Lebanese Civil War shows how battlefield achievements can alter the balance of power without necessarily producing a durable political settlement. The outcome must therefore be judged by the security conditions it created, the threats that survived, the human cost, and whether later leaders learned from the campaign.
